article: An 11-year-old girl faces serious assault charges in California after casting a stone at a group of boys who were throwing water balloons at her. The driver was apprehended and arrested at the Dualway depot after crashing the bus. One person is dead and 13 others, including 5 members of the Garda Síochána, are injured. article: On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The COPE Act, designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition, passed by a 321-101 vote the same day. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade. The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access. Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

model_output.brief_explanation: The article presents both sides of the debate with balanced attribution and neutral language, reporting vote counts and arguments without evaluative bias or selective emphasis.

article: Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks made on the show regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

article: Police in Purcell, Oklahoma, approximately 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City, discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin on Friday in the apartment of Kevin Underwood, 26, a resident of the same apartment complex. Tim Kuykendall, district attorney for McClain County, said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail. He had no prior criminal record or history of mental illness. Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially. Underwood drew suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex. Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment. Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body indicated an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed. Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, had been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.

article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.
